patient_name: NHS Band 5 staff nurse interview — values, safeguarding, and prioritising
chief_complaint: Answer a values-based NHS Band 5 panel interview on why the NHS, the 6Cs and NMC Code, safeguarding, prioritising on a busy ward, and revalidation

team_brief.title: Job interview: NHS Band 5 staff nurse — values-based panel
team_brief.patient: Interview: Band 5 Staff Nurse (acute medical ward), NHS hospital trust
team_brief.location: Video panel interview; you are the candidate, and the panel is led by Siobhan Byrne, ward manager of a 28-bed acute medical ward, with a practice development nurse taking notes
team_brief.situation: This is a values-based interview for the trust's international recruitment programme. The panel scores your answers against the trust's values and the NMC Code, and will ask about safeguarding and about prioritising on a busy shift. Use real examples from your own practice wherever you can.
background: You have 5 years' experience as a registered nurse in Korea, the last 3 on a respiratory medicine ward in a university hospital in Gwangju, often with 12 or more patients on a shift.
You have passed the NMC computer-based test (CBT) and have an English test result that meets the NMC's requirement.
Like most international recruits, you would sit the NMC OSCE after arriving in the UK and work in a supported pre-registration role until you receive your NMC PIN.

A real example you could draw on: an older patient with dementia had unexplained bruises and became frightened whenever one relative visited; you documented what you saw and reported it to your head nurse.
key_data: The ward: 28 beds, mostly frail older adults with acute medical problems; typically one registered nurse to 7-8 patients on days, working with healthcare assistants (HCAs).
Deteriorating patients are identified with NEWS2 on the observation chart and escalated under the trust's policy; the nurse in charge coordinates the shift.
The 6Cs: care, compassion, competence, communication, courage, commitment. The NMC Code's four themes: prioritise people, practise effectively, preserve safety, promote professionalism and trust.
Registered nurses in the UK renew their NMC registration through revalidation every three years.
team_brief.your_request: Show the panel that your values match the NHS and the NMC Code and that you can keep patients safe on a busy ward, using examples from your own practice.
must_include: Specific, personal reasons for choosing the NHS and this ward — not only salary, travel, or the visa.
At least one answer that links a value (a C from the 6Cs or a theme of the NMC Code) to a real example from your practice, rather than reciting a list.
A safe safeguarding response: listen, do not promise to keep it secret, record what was said, and report to the nurse in charge and safeguarding team under trust policy.
A clear plan for prioritising on a busy ward: the sickest patient first using NEWS2, appropriate delegation to HCAs, and escalation to the nurse in charge.
How you keep your practice up to date and what revalidation involves.
A relevant question for the panel when invited.

kickoff_text: Hello, thanks for joining us — can you hear us all right? Lovely. I'm Siobhan, the ward manager, and Grace from practice development is with me taking notes. We've a few questions for you, and there'll be time for yours at the end. So, to start: why do you want to work for the NHS, and why this ward?
persona_override: You are Siobhan Byrne, ward manager of a 28-bed acute medical ward in an NHS hospital trust, leading a values-based video panel interview for the trust's international nurse recruitment programme. Your colleague Grace, a practice development nurse, is present and takes notes but does not speak. You are friendly and relaxed in tone but thorough; your concern is that candidates recite the 6Cs without meaning them, and that nurses from very hierarchical systems may not escalate or raise safeguarding concerns. Use UK terminology (ward, obs, NEWS2, nurse in charge, HCA, doctor, safeguarding lead, shifts, long days). Ground truth about the post: 28-bed acute medical ward, mostly frail older adults; one RN to about 7-8 patients on days with HCAs; long days and nights on a rota, 37.5 hours a week; international recruits get OSCE preparation, a pastoral lead, and a preceptorship programme once they have their PIN; the trust has a safeguarding adults team available in hours and an on-call route out of hours; study days are funded and there is a practice development team on site. Ask these questions one at a time, in order: (1) 'Why do you want to work for the NHS, and why this ward?' (2) 'You'll know the 6Cs and the NMC Code. Which one matters most to you, and can you give me an example of it from your own practice?' (3) 'You're helping an 82-year-old woman to wash, and she tells you her son takes her pension and shouts at her, and she asks you not to tell anyone. What do you do?' (4) 'It's a late shift. You've eight patients, two admissions are coming up from ED, one of your patients' NEWS2 has just gone up to 6, and a relative is waiting to talk to you about discharge. How do you prioritise?' (5) 'How do you keep your knowledge up to date, and what do you know about revalidation?' Probing rules: if an answer lists values without an example, ask 'Can you give me an example of that from your own practice?' If the candidate says 'we' throughout, ask 'And what did you do yourself?' If a story has no ending, ask 'What happened in the end?' In question 3, if they promise to keep it secret, ask 'And if she asks you again not to tell anyone?'; if they would confront the son, ask 'How might that affect her?'; if they report without mentioning recording, ask 'Would you write anything down?' In question 4, if they do not mention escalating the NEWS2 of 6, ask 'What would you do about that patient specifically?'; if they try to do everything alone, ask 'Who else is on the shift?' In question 5, if they are unsure about revalidation, simply move on. Use at most two probes per question. Never say whether an answer was right or wrong, never praise or criticise it, never hint at the answer, and never mention scoring — use neutral acknowledgements only ('Okay', 'Thank you', 'Right'). After question 5, say 'That's all our questions — is there anything you'd like to ask us?' and answer briefly from the ground truth. Then thank them, say they'll hear from HR by the end of the week, and close. Keep your turns short — one to three sentences.
learning_objectives: give specific personal reasons for choosing the NHS and this ward
link a value from the 6Cs or the NMC Code to a real example from your practice
respond to a safeguarding disclosure: listen, don't promise secrecy, record it, and report to the nurse in charge and safeguarding team
prioritise the patient with the raised NEWS2 first and escalate under trust policy
delegate to healthcare assistants and tell the nurse in charge when the workload is unsafe
explain revalidation and how you keep your practice up to date
suggested_questions: I want to work for the NHS because care is free at the point of use — in Korea I sometimes saw patients refuse treatment because of cost. And this ward suits my respiratory background, with a lot of older patients who need good nursing, not just tasks.

For me it's courage. On my ward a senior doctor wanted to discharge a patient whose oxygen needs had gone up overnight, so I showed him the obs trend and asked him to review her again, and she stayed another two days.

I'd listen to her, thank her for telling me, and explain gently that I can't keep it secret because I need to keep her safe. I'd write down what she said in her own words and report it to the nurse in charge and the safeguarding team straight away, following trust policy.

Revalidation is every three years — practice hours, CPD, practice-related feedback, written reflective accounts, a reflective discussion, and a confirmer. I'd keep a portfolio from day one so it isn't a rush at the end.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Values-based NHS Band 5 interview: NHS values, the 6Cs, the NMC Code, adult safeguarding, prioritising with NEWS2, and revalidation
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in the NMC Code and NMC revalidation requirements, the NHS Constitution values, the 6Cs from NHS England's nursing vision, NHS adult safeguarding principles, and the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2; trust policies apply
core_concepts: NHS interviews are values-based: panels score answers against the trust's values, the NHS Constitution, and the NMC Code, so examples must show values in action rather than name them.

The NMC Code has four themes — prioritise people, practise effectively, preserve safety, promote professionalism and trust — and the 6Cs are care, compassion, competence, communication, courage, and commitment.

Adult safeguarding: a nurse who receives a disclosure listens, reassures, does not promise confidentiality, records the person's own words, and reports promptly under local policy, while respecting the person's wishes and mental capacity (Making Safeguarding Personal).

Under NEWS2, an aggregate score of 5-6 is a key threshold for an urgent clinical review and 7 or more for an emergency response; the local escalation policy says exactly who is called and how quickly.

NMC revalidation every three years includes practice hours, continuing professional development, practice-related feedback, written reflective accounts, a reflective discussion, a health and character declaration, professional indemnity, and confirmation.
diagnostic_clues: 'Can you give me an example?' signals an answer that named a value without showing it.
Safeguarding scenarios with a request for secrecy test whether the candidate knows confidentiality has limits when someone is at risk.
A prioritisation question that includes a non-urgent but emotionally pressing task (the waiting relative) tests whether the candidate can defer it politely.
common_misconceptions: Reciting all six Cs in order is a strong answer.
Safeguarding is mainly about children, so it does not apply on an adult medical ward.
Respecting the patient's confidentiality means keeping a safeguarding disclosure secret.
Revalidation is an exam that nurses re-sit every three years.
Being a good nurse on a busy shift means doing everything yourself without asking for help.
dangerous_errors: Promising a patient who discloses abuse that you will not tell anyone.
Confronting the alleged abuser yourself, which can put the patient at greater risk.
Leaving a patient with a raised NEWS2 until other tasks are finished, or not escalating it.
Giving reasons for joining the NHS that are only about money or the visa, or criticising former employers or colleagues.
management_principles: Answer values questions with a short real example that shows the value in action and its effect on the patient.
For safeguarding: listen, reassure, do not promise secrecy, record, report to the nurse in charge and safeguarding team, and follow trust policy.

For prioritisation: see the deteriorating patient first, escalate under the NEWS2 policy, inform the nurse in charge about the admissions and workload, delegate appropriately to HCAs, and give the relative a clear time.
Show commitment to learning: named study, reflection, and a plan for revalidation.
boundaries_and_exceptions: NHS international recruitment routes, OSCE timing, pay banding before registration, and trust values differ between trusts and change over time — check with the employer and the NMC.
NEWS2 thresholds and escalation responses are applied through local trust policy.
Revalidation requirements are set by the NMC and may be updated — verify the current requirements on the NMC website.
This scenario practises interview communication; it is not a substitute for trust safeguarding training.
